title: The first three petitions (CCC 2803–2827)
hook: thy name, thy kingdom, thy will

segments.voice: Yesterday, the whole gospel in a prayer: Tertullian's short summary, the Our Father. Your line was the whole gospel. Which Gospel story did the prayer bring to mind? Day one thousand one hundred forty-nine.

A wedding reception. The best man stands, taps a glass, and for the whole first part of his speech he doesn't mention himself once. It's all about the couple. Who they are. What they're building. What he hopes for them. Only near the end does he get to himself, and even then it's mostly a thank-you. Nobody in the room finds that strange. That's how speaking about someone you love tends to go. The Catechism notices the Our Father is built the same way. Before a single request for ourselves, three lines in a row turn toward God. Today: the first three petitions.
screen: `A TOAST AT A WEDDING.` → `THE COUPLE FIRST.` → `THREE LINES TURN TOWARD GOD.`

segments.voice: Listen to the little word that repeats. In the Douay-Rheims: "hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven." Thy, thy, thy. The Catechism says the prayer has seven petitions, and these first three draw us toward the Father's glory, for his own sake. It is the way of love, it says, to think first of the one we love. Take them one at a time. Thy name. To hallow means to hold as holy. The Catechism is careful here: we don't make God holy by saying it. God's name already is. We ask that it be recognized as holy, and kept holy in us, in the way we live. Thy kingdom. Jesus began his preaching with the kingdom at hand. The Catechism says this petition looks first toward the final coming of God's reign when Christ returns, and also toward that kingdom growing now, quietly, wherever people live by the Spirit. Thy will. Here the prayer meets Gethsemane. On the night of his arrest, Jesus prays there, "Father, if thou wilt, remove this chalice from me: but yet not my will, but thine be done." He asks for what he wants. Then he hands it over. And what is that will? The Catechism points to Paul's line: God "will have all men to be saved, and to come to the knowledge of the truth." So the first half of the Our Father isn't small talk before the real requests. In the Catholic reading, it reorders everything that comes after.
screen: `THY, THY, THY.` · `THY NAME: HOLD IT HOLY.` · `THY KINGDOM: COMING, AND NOW.` · `THY WILL: NOT MINE, BUT THINE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for his will. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing you want right now, honestly, the way Jesus did in the garden. Say it plainly, inside. Then, if you pray, you can add the words he used, "not my will, but thine be done," and leave a long silence after them. If you don't pray, simply loosen your grip on the thing a little, the way you'd open a closed hand. The bell holds the time.
The first three petitions. In the Our Father: hallowed be thy name, thy kingdom come, thy will be done, the requests that turn toward God first, for his own sake. Today's words.
Your line: thy, thy, thy. Today, in one conversation, try speaking about the other person first, before you get to what you need from them. Day one thousand one hundred forty-nine.

howItsDone: Catholics pray these three petitions every time they say the Our Father, at Mass, in the rosary and at home; some pause on 'thy will be done' when facing a hard decision.

original.note: Greek: let it be hallowed, held holy — the first petition of the Our Father in Matthew 6:9.

trapdoor: what you thought: the opening lines are a polite warm-up before the real requests.
what it means: the first three petitions turn toward God first, for his own sake: his name, his kingdom, his will.
what a scholar hears: the Catechism reads 'hallowed' as recognizing God's holiness, not causing it, and sets the third petition beside Gethsemane and 1 Timothy 2:4.
recall: a firm habit of doing good

notes: CCC 2803–2827 paraphrased (copyrighted English). Check: seven petitions, the first three drawing us toward the Father's glory (2803–2804), 'characteristic of love to think first of the one whom we love' (2804), hallowing as recognizing holiness, not causing it (2807, 2814), the kingdom petition referring primarily to Christ's return and also to the kingdom now (2818–2820), 1 Timothy 2:4 for the Father's will (2822), Gethsemane (2824).
The 'seven petitions' count is stated by CCC 2803; kept for that reason.
'Jesus began his preaching with the kingdom at hand' repeats yesterday's Matthew 4:17 without quoting it.
Douay-Rheims: confirm exact wording of Matthew 6:9–10, Luke 22:42 and 1 Timothy 2:4.
Editor pass: smoothed the repeated 'the night in the garden. In the garden' into one sentence naming Gethsemane; day 1148 no longer previews the Gethsemane line.
